title: Sparks from one fire
hook: as sparks fly from one fire and fall back into it, so beings come from the One (Akal Ustat 87)

segments.voice: Yesterday, same light in all: temple and mosque, the dress of different lands, and the same eyes underneath. Your line was all the same light. Where did you look one layer down? Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

Late at night at a bonfire, somebody drops another log on, and the fire answers. A column of sparks goes up into the dark. For a second each one is its own bright thing, drifting its own way, a little separate from the rest. Then they fade, and fall, and the ones that land in the coals simply become fire again. Kids watch this for a long time without being told to. The stanza right after yesterday's watches it too.
screen: `A LOG ON THE BONFIRE.` → `EACH SPARK ITS OWN WAY.` → `BACK INTO THE COALS.`

segments.voice: Akal Ustat, the next stanza, in paraphrase. As from one fire countless sparks rise up, and, each apart for a while, fall back into the fire. As from one heap of dust the particles fill the air, and settle back into the dust. As from one river countless waves rise, and the waves, being water, are all called water. So from the One, the form of all the world, beings appear; they arise from it, and into it they all merge again. Three pictures, one teaching. Look at what each one adds. The spark says: for a while you really are separate. Bright, moving, your own path through the dark. The stanza doesn't pretend that away. The dust says: even the small, plain, unglamorous bits come from the same heap. Not only the bright ones. And the wave says the boldest thing: even while it's rising, a wave never stops being water. You don't have to wait for the end to belong to the One. You're made of it now. One way Sikhs read it: this is the shape of a life. You come from the One, you live as a spark for a while, and you return. A few days ago, the ninth Guru's hymn ended with a person blending with the Lord like water into water. Here his son sings something close, in images of his own. It also finishes the thought of the last two days. One human race, the same light: here's why. Everyone you meet is a spark off the same fire.
screen: `SPARKS RISE AND FALL BACK.` · `DUST FROM ONE HEAP.` · `A WAVE IS STILL WATER.` · `FROM THE ONE, BACK TO THE ONE.` · then, large: `SPARKS OF ONE FIRE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch a flame. If you can, and it's safe to, light a candle, or open a video of a fire. If you can't, just close your eyes and remember one. Settle, and breathe. Watch how the flame moves and never quite holds a shape. Let yourself be one spark from it, bright for a while, on your own path. Then let the thought arrive: the same fire. If you pray, you can rest in Waheguru on each breath out. Put out any real flame when the bell sounds. The bell holds the time.
Sparks from one fire. Like sparks from a fire, dust from a heap, waves from a river, beings come from the One and merge in it again. Today's word.
Your line: sparks of one fire. Today, when someone gets on your nerves, think: same fire, different spark. Day one thousand two hundred twenty-six.

howItsDone: Sikhs sing this stanza of Akal Ustat in kirtan, and its images of sparks, dust and waves are used in katha to explain how all beings come from and return to the One.

fork.setup: a spark rises from the fire and drifts off into the dark. where, says the stanza, does it end up?
fork.reveal: the sparks, apart for a while, fall back into the fire. so beings come from the One and merge in it again.

original.note: a spark or particle, the word the stanza uses for the sparks and the specks of dust.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spark that flies off is gone.
what it means: in the stanza, beings rise from the One like sparks and merge back into it.
what a scholar hears: the wave image goes further: even while rising, a wave is called water.

notes: Akal Ustat 87 is paraphrased from memory; the text says 'kot' (crores) of sparks and waves, rendered here as 'countless'. Please check.
The Guru Granth Sahib parallel (water blending with water) is cited loosely to Sukhmani Sahib (jio jal mahi jal aae khataana); please supply the Ang or substitute a better reference.
The reading of each image (spark, dust, wave) is an interpretation offered in the teach, not the stanza's own gloss; please confirm it is fair.
